<br>

::: {.fragment fragment-index="4"}
**From a method for accurate matrix multiplication that was never expected to compete with FP64 on speed, to a potential FP64-killer**
:::

## Performance comes from hardware

::: fragment
**Integer slices don't reduce the work:** More slices ($3 \to 9$), more slice products
:::

::: fragment
**Speedups follow the hardware:** Faster than FP64 at 1 : 512 (consumer GPUs), slower at 1 : 32 (A100)
:::

<br>

::: fragment
**Hardware is trending in exactly the direction that accelerates the scheme.**
:::

## NVIDIA and FP64

::: fragment
NVIDIA cuts FP64 throughput: B200 37 → B300 1.3 TFLOP/s
:::

::: fragment
NVIDIA also ships FP64 emulation in cuBLAS, and authors most of its evaluations.
:::

::: fragment
Meanwhile, AMD's MI250X and MI300A (Frontier and El Capitan) keep strong FP64 throughput.
:::

<br>

::: fragment
**Emulation is most attractive exactly where FP64 has been deprioritized.**
:::

## What we can conclude

::: fragment
Every speedup: On hardware where FP64 has been deprioritized for AI
:::

::: fragment
Every accuracy test before DMRG: Synthetic matrices, with one magnitude-range parameter
:::

<br>

::: fragment
**"FP8 is all you need": The evidence in these works does not support the claim that emulation can largely replace native FP64.**
:::

::: fragment
It supports the moderate position: The Ozaki scheme is a useful tool where it is useful.
:::

## Future work

- A systematic characterization of how the scheme fails, on structured and real-application matrices
- A clearer picture of memory overhead in full applications
- Automatic slice-count selection below the FP64-equivalent bound: The scheme as a variable-precision method
- Lightweight heuristics for deciding when to emulate
